segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now before the Passover festival, Jesus knew that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to hand him over,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: got up from supper, laid down his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he poured water into the basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to dry them with the towel he had tied around him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he came to Simon Peter, who said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, are you going to wash my feet?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You will never wash my feet!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The one who has bathed has no need to wash anything except the feet, but is clean all over. And you are clean, but not all of you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he knew who was handing him over; that is why he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Not all of you are clean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he had washed their feet and taken up his outer garments and reclined at the table again, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you understand what I have done for you?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You call me ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord,’ and you are right to say so, for I am.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So if I, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I have given you an example, so that you also should do just as I have done for you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly, truly, I tell you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is so that the Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘The one who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am telling you this now, before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe that I am he.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever receives anyone I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After saying this, Jesus was troubled in spirit and testified,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will hand me over.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples looked at one another, at a loss as to which one he meant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of his disciples, the one Jesus loved, was reclining at the table at Jesus’s side.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Simon Peter nodded to this disciple to ask who it was that he was speaking about.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Leaning back, just as he was, against Jesus’s chest, that disciple said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, who is it?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is the one for whom I will dip the piece of bread and give it to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he dipped the piece of bread and gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And after the piece of bread, Satan then entered into him. So Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What you are doing, do quickly.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But none of those reclining at the table knew why he said this to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some thought that, since Judas kept the money box, Jesus was telling him to buy what they needed for the festival, or to give something to the poor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So after taking the piece of bread, he went out at once. And it was night.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had gone out, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him at once.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. You will look for me, and just as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say it to you too.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I give you a new commandment: that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, where are you going?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow later.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, why can’t I follow you right now? I will lay down my life for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I tell you, a rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.”

notes.note: The Greek phrase can mean “to the end” in time (to the last moment of his life) or “to the utmost,” that is, completely. Many interpreters think John intends both, and the phrase is echoed in Jesus’s final word from the cross, “It is finished” (19:30). “To the end” is kept because English can hear both senses in it.

Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same verb for what the chief priests and Pilate later do to Jesus. “Hand over” lets that chain show. The treachery comes from the context, though some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual sense.

notes.traditional: put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him
notes.note: The best-attested Greek text says literally that the devil had already put “into the heart that Judas son of Simon Iscariot should hand him over,” without saying whose heart. Most translations take it as Judas’s heart, as here. Some scholars read it as the devil’s own heart, meaning the devil had already resolved that Judas would do this, with Satan entering Judas only at verse 27. Later manuscripts adjust the grammar so that the heart is plainly Judas’s.

The verbs for “laying down” the garments here and “taking them up” in verse 12 are the ones Jesus uses in 10:17–18 for laying down his life and taking it up again, and Peter uses the first in verse 37. Many commentators think the echo is deliberate, so the translation keeps the same English verbs, though not all agree that John intends a symbol here.

A few early witnesses lack the words “except the feet,” giving “The one who has bathed has no need to wash, but is clean all over.” Most manuscripts include the words, as does the Greek text translated here. Scholars are divided over which form is original.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired servant, and “master” here is the same Greek word translated “Lord” in verses 13–14. Many English versions soften it to “servant.” Several recent translations use “slave,” as here.

The Greek word is the one usually rendered “apostle,” and this is its only occurrence in John’s Gospel. Here it has its ordinary sense of someone sent on another’s behalf, paired with “the one who sent him.”

notes.phrase: has lifted his heel against me
notes.note: The quotation is from Psalm 41:9, where the psalmist laments being turned on by a close friend who shared his table. In the ancient world eating someone’s bread created a bond of loyalty, so an attack from a table companion was an especially bitter treachery. The exact picture behind “lifting the heel” is uncertain; it may be a kick or a gesture of contempt.

The Greek is simply “I am,” with no “he.” It can be an everyday way of saying “I am the one,” but in the Greek version of Isaiah (for example 43:10, “that you may know and believe … that I am”) it is God’s own self-declaration. Many scholars think John intends that echo here. Others take it more simply as “that I am who I claim to be.”

Guests at a formal meal reclined on their left side on cushions, so that the head of one diner lay near the chest of the person to his left. The Greek says this disciple was reclining “in the bosom of Jesus,” the place of a close companion, and John uses the same word in 1:18 for the Son’s closeness to the Father. “Bosom” is no longer natural English.

notes.phrase: If God has been glorified in him,
notes.note: This opening clause is missing from several of the earliest and most important manuscripts and present in the majority of later ones. It may have been dropped accidentally because it repeats the end of the previous sentence, or added to smooth the logic. The Greek text translated here includes it, and the sense of the passage is little affected either way.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the whole New Testament and versions split between “slave” and “servant,” which changes how readers hear both parables and Paul’s self-descriptions.
The same word serves as “Lord,” “master” and “sir,” and the choice (for example in address to Jesus or in sayings like v. 16) needs a consistent policy so wordplay is not lost.
The dining verbs (with ἀναπίπτω, κατάκειμαι) recur throughout the Gospels and versions vary between “recline,” “sit at table” and “sit down,” obscuring the meal custom.
Occurs widely as “cloak,” “garment,” “clothes” or “robe”; a fixed policy for singular (cloak) and plural (clothes/garments) would keep passages aligned.
John’s absolute “I am” sayings (8:24, 8:28, 8:58, 13:19, 18:5–6) need one decision on whether to supply “he” so the echo of the Isaianic divine self-declaration is handled uniformly.
